news.exam_corner_topic: She made India fall in love with women's cricket - now her era as captain is over
news.headline: She made India fall in love with women's cricket - now her era as captain is over
news.story_lead: Harmanpreet Kaur is stepping down as the captain of the India women's cricket team - Published 8 October 2026 When Harmanpreet Kaur scored that unforgettable World Cup century against Australia in the 2017 semi-final, she not only changed the course of a match but the trajectory of women's cricket in India. India went on to lose the final to England that year but women's cricket no longer remained a passing pursuit for the average Indian fan. That dogged zeal to win she infused into the team helped them lift India's first women's World Cup trophy - the same feat that had eluded them in 2017 - in emphatic fashion eight years later.
news.full_article_text: Harmanpreet Kaur is stepping down as the captain of the India women's cricket team - Published 8 October 2026 When Harmanpreet Kaur scored that unforgettable World Cup century against Australia in the 2017 semi-final, she not only changed the course of a match but the trajectory of women's cricket in India. India went on to lose the final to England that year but women's cricket no longer remained a passing pursuit for the average Indian fan. That dogged zeal to win she infused into the team helped them lift India's first women's World Cup trophy - the same feat that had eluded them in 2017 - in emphatic fashion eight years later. Less than a year on, and within weeks of victories in the Asia Cup and the Asian Games, she has relinquished the captaincy, ending an era in which she became the team's most influential leader and one of the most recognisable figures in the sport. Star opener Smriti Mandhana, her long-time deputy, has been appointed captain across all formats. Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) secretary Devajit Saikia, coach Amol Muzumdar, Harmanpreet and Mandhana attended the review meeting at which the leadership change was ratified. The transition, however, was not entirely seamless. Reports suggest the 37-year-old Harmanpreet was willing to relinquish the T20 captaincy immediately, but was keen to continue leading the side in One-Day Internationals and Tests so that younger players could benefit from her experience. The BCCI, however, was intent on a younger person at the helm and opted for the 30-year-old Mandhana. In some ways, the move mirrors the BCCI's decision to replace Suryakumar Yadav as captain of the men's T20 side shortly after India won the World Cup earlier this year, with the captaincy passing to Shreyas Iyer. Harmanpreet's future as captain had become a subject of intense debate in cricketing circles after India's below-par performance at the T20 World Cup in England a few months ago. Her own poor form with the bat amplified concerns and prompted the BCCI to consider changes that could help the team meet the growing challenges of a women's game that continues to expand rapidly around the world. Approaching her 38th birthday, and after almost a decade at the helm, Harmanpreet found herself under increasing scrutiny as her form dipped. Harmanpreet led the India women's team to a famous World Cup win in 2025 Opinion on whether she should continue as captain was sharply divided among former women players and captains. Former cricketer Diana Edulji, among the most respected names in the game, felt Harmanpreet had done everything that could reasonably have been expected of her and that it was time for a younger captain to take over. Former captain Anjum Chopra, meanwhile, argued that Harmanpreet's experience remained invaluable and that she should stay on. Sensing that the BCCI was strongly inclined towards a change, Harmanpreet opted to step down during the review meeting. She later announced her decision in an emotional Instagram post. "I feel I have done my duty. I gave this team everything I had," she wrote. "Now, it is time for me to turn the pageâ¦ Blood. Sweat. Sacrifice. Pride. I gave it all. Now, I'm ready to play for the love of the game again. "Captaincy ends, the journey continues." Harmanpreet's intention to continue playing now leaves the BCCI with another decision to make about her future. In Suryakumar Yadav's case, he not only lost the captaincy but also his place in India's T20 side. Given the depth of talent available in the men's game, it was easier for Ajit Agarkar and his fellow selectors to take what was always likely to be a contentious decision. The situation in the women's game is different. Despite Harmanpreet's modest recent form, replacing a player of her experience and stature may not be straightforward, as the talent pipeline is not yet as deep as it is in men's cricket. Whatever the future holds, Harmanpreet has scripted among the more memorable careers in women's cricket. Spanning more than two decades, it is a journey marked by significant achievements and milestones. Harmanpreet (left) has now passed the captaincy baton to Smriti Mandhana (right) Born into a family of modest means in Punjab's Moga city, Harmanpreet developed a passion for cricket at an early age. Her family's support was vital in the early years, but her rise to national recognition came after she joined the Railways - a transition facilitated by Diana Edulji - and moved to Mumbai. The superior facilities and greater professionalism associated with Mumbai's sporting culture helped accelerate her development. She made her India debut in 2009 at the age of 20 and has remained an integral part of the national side across formats ever since. An all-rounder for the better part of her first decade in cricket, she made herself indispensable to the side with her explosive middle-order batting, crafty off-spin and sharp fielding skills. Her blistering century against Australia in the semi-final of the 2017 Women's ODI World Cup remains one of the defining knocks in the history of the women's game. India went on to lose to England in the final, but beating Australia was a monumental hurdle overcome. That century also helped spark wider interest in women's cricket in India, and transformed Harmanpreet into a household name. Harmanpreet made her debut in the India women's cricket team in 2009 The second decade of her career showcased her prowess both as batter and captain. Having succeeded Mithali Raj as T20 captain in 2016, Harmanpreet assumed charge across all formats in 2022 and went on to guide India to some of the greatest successes in its history. Her leadership was marked by an aggressive pursuit of victory. That fearless approach instilled confidence and ambition in her teammates, helping the team overcome even the previously unbeatable Australians, most memorably in the semi-final of the 2025 ODI World Cup. Unlike in 2017, Harmanpreet couldn't get a hundred on that occasion, but her innings of 89 was a stellar effort as captain. Combined with Jemimah Rodrigues's century, it helped India secure a famous victory over their arch rivals. India then defeated South Africa in the final to reach what many regard as the pinnacle of achievement in the history of Indian women's cricket. With multiple titles and trophies won under her leadership, Harmanpreet leaves behind a formidable legacy for her successor, Smriti Mandhana, to emulate. Related topics

news.headline: Karnataka asks hospitals to reveal medicine purchase prices, display procedure costs
news.story_lead: Karnataka asks hospitals to reveal medicine purchase prices, display procedure costs The measures are intended to give patients a clearer account of medicine costs and bring greater transparency to hospital billing. From November 1, patients at hospitals across Karnataka will be able to see what hospitals paid for medicines as well as their maximum retail prices, under new billing requirements announced by the state government. Karnataka health and family welfare minister U T Khader said in Bengaluru that hospitals in the state will have to record both figures on patient bills and use the disclosed prices while charging for medicines.
news.full_article_text: Karnataka asks hospitals to reveal medicine purchase prices, display procedure costs The measures are intended to give patients a clearer account of medicine costs and bring greater transparency to hospital billing. From November 1, patients at hospitals across Karnataka will be able to see what hospitals paid for medicines as well as their maximum retail prices, under new billing requirements announced by the state government. Karnataka health and family welfare minister U T Khader said in Bengaluru that hospitals in the state will have to record both figures on patient bills and use the disclosed prices while charging for medicines. Medicine price lists will also have to be displayed in prominent public areas, particularly near registration counters. The government is also considering greater disclosure of procedure costs. Hospitals could display prices for major medical procedures on notice boards, while charges for other procedures could be maintained in a ledger that patients could consult when required, Khader said. The proposed rules will not require private hospitals to adopt the rates charged at government facilities. Instead, Khader said private hospital charges could vary depending on the amenities and level of treatment provided. “We are not expecting the pricing at private hospitals to be on par with the price set at government hospitals, but the rates could be fixed based on the amenities provided and the level of treatment at the hospital,” he said. The government’s proposed changes will therefore cover not only the disclosure of medicine purchase prices and MRPs on bills, but also the public display of medicine prices and, potentially, procedure charges. No punishment for violation yet The state has yet to decide what action hospitals could face for failing to comply with the new requirements. The Health Department plans to meet private hospitals shortly to discuss and finalise the terms and conditions. “The punishment for violating the rules would be discussed,” U T Khader said. He said the government did not want regulations to make healthcare businesses financially unviable, while arguing that tighter rules were necessary. “We do not intend to push the healthcare business into loss, but some stringent rules and regulations will have to be put in place,” he said. Minister blames foreign investment for rising healthcare costs Khader said the government was concerned about the rise in healthcare costs and, in his view, linked part of the increase to the entry of foreign investors into the healthcare sector. “According to my observation, after foreign investors have entered the healthcare market, the prices have gone up tremendously. We will discuss and see what best can be done,” he said. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Arun Dev Arun Dev is an Assistant Editor with the Karnataka bureau of Hindustan Times. A journalist for over 10 years, he has written extensively on crime and politics.

news.headline: No dilution in prescribed standards: NMC on denotification of medical education regulations
news.story_lead: No dilution in prescribed standards: NMC on denotification of medical education regulations New Delhi, The National Medical Commission has asserted that the de-notification of the Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations, 2023 will not dilute prescribed standards of medical education and are intended to remove overlapping procedures. The Commission, which is the statutory body for medical education in the country, had on October 14 denotified the Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations . The denotification "does not, in any manner, dilute the prescribed standards of medical education or the regulatory oversight exercised by NMC," a statement by the Commission said.

news.full_article_text: ‘You are responsible for this mess’: Piyush Goyal slams West over carbon emissions, climate finance failures Goyal reminded the developed countries of the pledge to provide financial and technological support to developing nations under the Paris Agreement Union commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal blamed developed countries for contributing a disproportionately large share of global carbon emissions while failing to honour the climate finance commitments they made at COP21 in Paris in 2015. Speaking at a roundtable during the Berlin Global Dialogue, Goyal said Western countries were largely responsible for the environmental damage caused by ozone layer depletion and carbon emissions. He also told the roundtable that India's contribution to global carbon emissions was only three to four percentage points lower than Europe's, despite India having a population of 1.4 billion and accounting for 17 per cent of the world's population. Also Read | Emissions didn't spike in 2025. That doesn't mean climate crisis has been stopped in its tracks "Who's responsible for this mess in the first place? Where did the ozone layer get damaged? Who sent all that carbon into the atmosphere? I represent 17% of the world's population, but my contribution to global carbon emissions is less than 3%. You (Europe) represent probably 3% or 4% of the world's population, yet your contribution to those carbon emissions—or this mess—is humongous. The problem was caused by you," Goyal said. Goyal said India's per capita carbon emissions remain significantly lower than those of Western countries, arguing that Europe’s per capita emissions and environmental impact are seven to eight times higher than India's. “Even today, as we sit here, my per capita contribution to carbon emissions is probably less than 10 per cent or 15 per cent of yours. Even today, Europe's per capita contribution to carbon emissions—and its per capita environmental impact—is probably seven or eight times that of India,” Goyal said. Also Read | If current policies continue, warming could reach 2.8°C within this century: UN report What happened to $100 billion climate finance pledge, Goyal questions? Goyal also reminded the developed countries of the world about the pledge to provide financial and technological support to developing and vulnerable nations under the Paris Agreement. He said that as per the agreement, developed countries were to assist developing countries with climate finance worth $100 billion but not a ‘dime of it’ has been received. "At the Paris climate conference in 2015, when the whole world came together, it was Prime Minister Modi who brought the Global South together and encouraged countries to commit to addressing climate change at COP21. It was agreed that the developed countries, who have enjoyed the fruits of messing up the climate for so many decades, will pay a greater price, and will support the developing and less developed countries, as well as island nations in the Pacific and the Caribbean...Just $100 billion a year. That was the commitment," Goyal said. Also Read | Ahead of COP31 next month, what has India committed to and what does it expect? “Eleven years later, we haven't seen a nickel or a dime of that. It's all promises. The larger question that the European Union and CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism) have failed to answer,” Goyal added. India reportedly recorded a decline in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in 2025 compared to the previous year, breaking a prolonged trend of rapid growth, according to the United Nations Environment Programme's (UNEP) annual Emissions Gap Report released on Wednesday. The decline was attributed partly to weather-related factors and partly to structural shifts towards renewable energy. news.story_lead: India-US trade deal in ‘last stage’, says EAM Jaishankar: ‘It’s never done until it’s done’ The trade deal figured in Jaishankar’s meeting with Rubio this week after the secretary of state visited India for the second time in less than five months. The India-US trade agreement is in its “last mile” but “it’s never done till it’s done”, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said on Thursday about efforts by the two countries to find common ground on the deal they have negotiated for more than a year. US secretary of state Marco Rubio and commerce minister Piyush Goyal too have spoken of the two sides moving towards the final stages of the trade deal, he said at a session at the NDTV World Summit.

US secretary of state Marco Rubio and commerce minister Piyush Goyal too have spoken of the two sides moving towards the final stages of the trade deal, he said at a session at the NDTV World Summit. “But…often the last mile or the penultimate miles do pose their challenges. I think the [negotiating] teams are working through them now,” Jaishankar said. “If you’re asking me to tell you what exactly those challenges are, I’m sorry I won’t. Bilateral ties have been hit by the Trump administration’s unpredictable trade policies, immigration restrictions that have impacted Indian professionals and growing ties between Washington and the Pakistani military leadership. Jaishankar said he failed to understand criticism by opposition parties of his visit to Mumbai to meet Rubio, which Congress leader Rahul Gandhi had described as a “summoning”. “They have something against Mumbai. It’s our financial capital, it’s our Bollywood capital. It has got so much going for it. Maybe Mumbai doesn’t like them, I have no idea why they have this reservation,” the minister said. Jaishankar listed examples of Indian leaders travelling out of New Delhi to meet foreign dignitaries, including two instances involving Congress leaders – former PM Indira Gandhi met Pakistani leader Zulfikar Ali Bhutto in Shimla in 1972 to sign the Simla Agreement, and Union minister Salman Khurshid hosted a lunch for then Pakistan PM Raja Pervez Ashraf in Jaipur in 2013. “We are adults, let’s have an adult conversation,” he said, taking a swipe at Rahul Gandhi. On Pakistan and terrorism Jaishankar also spoke on the issue of Pakistan-backed terrorism and said India does not want to wait for the US and other countries to understand its concerns on terror. He emphasised that the world takes note only when a country responds to terrorism, and India has done so through Operation Sindoor and the Balakot air strikes. While India desires good relations with Pakistan, it is unwilling to overlook terrorism to achieve this, he said. He responded to a question on Pakistan’s military leadership wooing the Trump administration in the US and the perception that Washington hasn’t fully understood New Delhi’s concerns on cross-border terror by saying the issue is much broader. “If Washington understood it so well, why didn’t we act in 2008, when 26/11 happened? And when we did act, we didn’t act because Washington understood it, we acted because we understood it,” he said. “First of all, forget about somebody else getting terrorism right. Get it right yourself. If you don’t have the clarity of thought, the conviction to fight back against terrorism, don’t think somebody else is going to do that job for you.” Also Read I ‘India diversified imports, but hard to pivot in one day’: Marco Rubio explains why US waived some Russia energy tariffs India’s counter-terror policy has evolved and this was evident in the response to cross-border terror with last year’s Operation Sindoor, the Balakot air strikes in 2019, and the surgical strikes across the Line of Control in 2016. “The evolution is that if terrorism goes on, it will not be business as usual. It is not, you will take a break and then say, ‘Okay, now it has been a long time. Let me get back to talking to them again’, which is what the pattern was,” he said. “The 26/11 attacks should serve as a reminder of the enormity of what is being done to us and the necessity for us to respond. And when you respond, the world will take note. When you don’t respond, the world will play games.” When Jaishankar was asked if India, which has made it clear that terrorism and talks cannot go together, still wishes to have better relations with Pakistan, he said the reality was Islamabad was using terrorism as state policy. “Of course we want good relations with Pakistan, we want that with all our neighbours but will I overlook terror for that? I will not. The government is very clear,” he said. “The national mood on Pakistan changed after 26/11. Till then, there were people who would keep making these arguments. After 26/11, only the government of the day made the argument.” United Nations and protests Jaishankar responded to another question on whether the UN has “double standards” on protests in different countries by saying that the answer is “pretty obvious”. The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and UN human rights experts have expressed concern over the government’s handling of protests associated with the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) and other groups. “That is a bigger issue because you get into what the UN is, what positions they take, and so forth. Let’s be straightforward about it, I am making this assessment and observation about what is happening across multiple countries and societies. This is not a comment specific to India, the Indian subcontinent or France,” Jaishankar said. “We have seen that in many cases, when these moments occur, there is external encouragement and external support. There is a set of actors who see this as a tool of influence to advance their agenda. It is not a secret – even those who do it openly admit to it, they are not hiding it,” he said. He said he watches The Diplomat on Netflix but noted that the series presents diplomacy in a distinctly American way. “I’m watching The Diplomat but I want to say one thing. news.full_article_text: India, Poland pledge to deepen ties in defence, nuclear energy New Delhi India and Poland on Thursday agreed to deepen cooperation in defence, space and nuclear energy as Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Polish counterpart Donald Tusk focused on leveraging the economic growth of both countries to achieve the shared target of doubling trade from the current level of $6 billion by 2030 New Delhi India and Poland on Thursday agreed to deepen cooperation in defence, space and nuclear energy as Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Polish counterpart Donald Tusk focused on leveraging the economic growth of both countries to achieve the shared target of doubling trade from the current level of $6 billion by 2030. Bilateral ties got a major boost with Modi’s visit to Warsaw in 2024, the first by an Indian PM in 45 years, and defence and security have emerged as a key area for cooperation as Poland is currently engaged in the largest military modernisation campaign in Europe by spending almost 5% of its GDP on its armed forces against the backdrop of the war in Ukraine. Modi described his discussions with Tusk as “excellent” and said on social media the two leaders discussed bolstering cooperation in trade, investment, defence, nuclear energy, space and critical minerals. Regional and global issues also figured in the talks, and Indian officials said the Polish side appreciated India’s recent proposal for a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire. “Today, we agreed to deepen our cooperation in defence, space and nuclear energy. In all these strategic sectors, we invite Polish companies to partner with India in co-development and co-production,” Modi said at a media interaction with Tusk. Tusk added, “We are very aware of political threats and the need to become independent as much as possible in the area of…minerals and strategic resources…to make sure that Poland and India are independent in those areas.” India and Poland, Modi said, have emerged as centres of growth and technology at a time of uncertainty and change. “Last year, Poland’s GDP crossed the historic milestone of $1 trillion…Meanwhile, India recorded an impressive growth rate of 7.8% in the last quarter,” he said, noting that the proposed India-European Union (EU) trade deal will open new opportunities for India to export machinery, chemicals, plastics and engineering goods to Poland. “At the same time, we will seek new investments from Poland in sectors such as railways and mobility, advanced manufacturing, food processing and biotechnology,” Modi said, adding that Tusk is accompanied by a large business delegation that will focus on developing trusted supply chains to achieve the shared goal of doubling trade by 2030. The two sides will also develop new partnerships in critical minerals and coal gasification using Polish expertise, and establish a bilateral “startup bridge” to build on cooperation in AI, cybersecurity and fintech, Modi said. The business delegation of almost 100 Polish companies will participate in two business forums in New Delhi and Bengaluru to explore collaboration in defence, agri-tech, food processing, pharmaceuticals, mining, technology and infrastructure. Two-way trade is currently worth $6.3 billion, and Indian investments in Poland have grown to $3 billion, with Indian IT companies having a significant presence. Tusk noted the two countries were able to build synergy as they have no conflicts of interest or historical issues that divide them. He also lauded Modi’s role on the global stage, describing it as a “beacon of hope” at a time of destabilisation and political uncertainty. He pointed to growing defence cooperation between the two sides and said: “Our drones were very useful…recently and I am convinced that cooperation in satellites and drones has helped our countries in times of political tensions and crises.” Tusk’s comments were an apparent reference to the use of Polish loitering munitions or drones by India’s military against Pakistan during Operation Sindoor, last year’s campaign that targeted terrorist infrastructure on Pakistani soil in retaliation for the Pahalgam attack. Poland’s WB Group supplied 100 units of Warmate loitering munitions to the Indian Army in 2022, and Polish officials said earlier this year that the army had signed three more defence contracts. Poland is also eyeing tie-ups with Indian manufacturers of munitions to replenish ammunition stocks depleted by supplies provided to Ukraine since the start of the Russian invasion in 2022. However, some Polish firms have concerns about India’s long-standing military ties with Russia, and New Delhi and Warsaw are finalising an agreement on secure information exchanges to boost defence industrial cooperation. Sibi George, secretary (West) in the external affairs ministry, told a media briefing the two sides are working on an agreement on mutual protection and exchange of classified information that is expected to build on the growing trust between India and the EU in areas such as defence and technology. With both countries eyeing joint development and production of military gear, it is important to have agreements to put in place trust and confidentiality, he said. The two sides also agreed to establish a defence industry dialogue and a counter-terrorism dialogue, George said. The security and defence partnership concluded by India and the EU earlier this year provides an additional framework for strategic cooperation with Poland in defence, counter-terrorism, technology, cybersecurity, space and shipbuilding, he said. Modi also referred to his discussions with Tusk on regional and global issues and said: “Whether in Ukraine or West Asia, India will continue to support every meaningful effort towards peace.” George said Poland was “very appreciative” of India’s approach for a diplomatic solution to the Russia-Ukraine conflict, and Modi’s recent call to Russian President Vladimir Putin to move from “endless war to the end of war”. He added that India has shared ideas with Russia and Ukraine, including the safety and security of commercial shipping, exports of grains and energy, and “non-attack possibilities”. Modi and Tusk both highlighted people-to-people ties, including the role played by the royal families of Jamnagar and Kolhapur in providing refuge to thousands of Polish children and families during World War II, and the assistance provided by Polish authorities in evacuating thousands of Indian students from Ukraine in 2022. New Delhi India and Poland on Thursday agreed to deepen cooperation in defence, space and nuclear energy as Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Polish counterpart Donald Tusk focused on leveraging the economic growth of both countries to achieve the shared target of doubling trade from the current level of $6 billion by 2030.

Bilateral ties got a major boost with Modi’s visit to Warsaw in 2024, the first by an Indian PM in 45 years, and defence and security have emerged as a key area for cooperation as Poland is currently engaged in the largest military modernisation campaign in Europe by spending almost 5% of its GDP on its armed forces against the backdrop of the war in Ukraine.

Modi described his discussions with Tusk as “excellent” and said on social media the two leaders discussed bolstering cooperation in trade, investment, defence, nuclear energy, space and critical minerals. Regional and global issues also figured in the talks, and Indian officials said the Polish side appreciated India’s recent proposal for a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire.

“Today, we agreed to deepen our cooperation in defence, space and nuclear energy. In all these strategic sectors, we invite Polish companies to partner with India in co-development and co-production,” Modi said at a media interaction with Tusk.

hindi_translation.full_article_text: India, Poland pledge to deepen ties in defence, nuclear energy New Delhi India and Poland on Thursday agreed to deepen cooperation in defence, space and nuclear energy as Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Polish counterpart Donald Tusk focused on leveraging the economic growth of both countries to achieve the shared target of doubling trade from the current level of $6 billion by 2030 New Delhi India and Poland on Thursday agreed to deepen cooperation in defence, space and nuclear energy as Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Polish counterpart Donald Tusk focused on leveraging the economic growth of both countries to achieve the shared target of doubling trade from the current level of $6 billion by 2030. Bilateral ties got a major boost with Modi’s visit to Warsaw in 2024, the first by an Indian PM in 45 years, and defence and security have emerged as a key area for cooperation as Poland is currently engaged in the largest military modernisation campaign in Europe by spending almost 5% of its GDP on its armed forces against the backdrop of the war in Ukraine. Modi described his discussions with Tusk as “excellent” and said on social media the two leaders discussed bolstering cooperation in trade, investment, defence, nuclear energy, space and critical minerals. Regional and global issues also figured in the talks, and Indian officials said the Polish side appreciated India’s recent proposal for a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire. “Today, we agreed to deepen our cooperation in defence, space and nuclear energy. In all these strategic sectors, we invite Polish companies to partner with India in co-development and co-production,” Modi said at a media interaction with Tusk. Tusk added, “We are very aware of political threats and the need to become independent as much as possible in the area of…minerals and strategic resources…to make sure that Poland and India are independent in those areas.” India and Poland, Modi said, have emerged as centres of growth and technology at a time of uncertainty and change. “Last year, Poland’s GDP crossed the historic milestone of $1 trillion…Meanwhile, India recorded an impressive growth rate of 7.8% in the last quarter,” he said, noting that the proposed India-European Union (EU) trade deal will open new opportunities for India to export machinery, chemicals, plastics and engineering goods to Poland. “At the same time, we will seek new investments from Poland in sectors such as railways and mobility, advanced manufacturing, food processing and biotechnology,” Modi said, adding that Tusk is accompanied by a large business delegation that will focus on developing trusted supply chains to achieve the shared goal of doubling trade by 2030. The two sides will also develop new partnerships in critical minerals and coal gasification using Polish expertise, and establish a bilateral “startup bridge” to build on cooperation in AI, cybersecurity and fintech, Modi said. The business delegation of almost 100 Polish companies will participate in two business forums in New Delhi and Bengaluru to explore collaboration in defence, agri-tech, food processing, pharmaceuticals, mining, technology and infrastructure. Two-way trade is currently worth $6.3 billion, and Indian investments in Poland have grown to $3 billion, with Indian IT companies having a significant presence. Tusk noted the two countries were able to build synergy as they have no conflicts of interest or historical issues that divide them. He also lauded Modi’s role on the global stage, describing it as a “beacon of hope” at a time of destabilisation and political uncertainty. He pointed to growing defence cooperation between the two sides and said: “Our drones were very useful…recently and I am convinced that cooperation in satellites and drones has helped our countries in times of political tensions and crises.” Tusk’s comments were an apparent reference to the use of Polish loitering munitions or drones by India’s military against Pakistan during Operation Sindoor, last year’s campaign that targeted terrorist infrastructure on Pakistani soil in retaliation for the Pahalgam attack. Poland’s WB Group supplied 100 units of Warmate loitering munitions to the Indian Army in 2022, and Polish officials said earlier this year that the army had signed three more defence contracts. Poland is also eyeing tie-ups with Indian manufacturers of munitions to replenish ammunition stocks depleted by supplies provided to Ukraine since the start of the Russian invasion in 2022. However, some Polish firms have concerns about India’s long-standing military ties with Russia, and New Delhi and Warsaw are finalising an agreement on secure information exchanges to boost defence industrial cooperation. Sibi George, secretary (West) in the external affairs ministry, told a media briefing the two sides are working on an agreement on mutual protection and exchange of classified information that is expected to build on the growing trust between India and the EU in areas such as defence and technology. With both countries eyeing joint development and production of military gear, it is important to have agreements to put in place trust and confidentiality, he said. The two sides also agreed to establish a defence industry dialogue and a counter-terrorism dialogue, George said. The security and defence partnership concluded by India and the EU earlier this year provides an additional framework for strategic cooperation with Poland in defence, counter-terrorism, technology, cybersecurity, space and shipbuilding, he said. Modi also referred to his discussions with Tusk on regional and global issues and said: “Whether in Ukraine or West Asia, India will continue to support every meaningful effort towards peace.” George said Poland was “very appreciative” of India’s approach for a diplomatic solution to the Russia-Ukraine conflict, and Modi’s recent call to Russian President Vladimir Putin to move from “endless war to the end of war”. He added that India has shared ideas with Russia and Ukraine, including the safety and security of commercial shipping, exports of grains and energy, and “non-attack possibilities”. Modi and Tusk both highlighted people-to-people ties, including the role played by the royal families of Jamnagar and Kolhapur in providing refuge to thousands of Polish children and families during World War II, and the assistance provided by Polish authorities in evacuating thousands of Indian students from Ukraine in 2022. Poland is currently home to around 30,000 Indians, including 3,500 students. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Rezaul H Laskar Rezaul Hasan Laskar is Foreign Editor with the Hindustan Times, which he joined in 2015. He began as a journalist in his hometown of Shillong in northeast India and has worked in newspapers and wire services over the years. news.exam_corner_topic: Telangana to host first state-organised defence and aerospace expo, curtain-raiser on Saturday
news.headline: Telangana to host first state-organised defence and aerospace expo, curtain-raiser on Saturday
news.story_lead: Telangana to host first state-organised defence and aerospace expo, curtain-raiser on Saturday The main event, scheduled from December 7 to 9 will bring together the aerospace, space, defence, and internal security sectors on a single platform. Telangana is set to host Raksha Expo 2026—India’s first defence and aerospace expo organised by a state government—with the curtain-raiser scheduled to be held in Hyderabad on October 24. The main event, scheduled from December 7 to 9 at Bharat Future City, will bring together the aerospace, space, defence, and internal security sectors on a single platform to promote domestic manufacturing, innovation, and investment.
news.full_article_text: Telangana to host first state-organised defence and aerospace expo, curtain-raiser on Saturday The main event, scheduled from December 7 to 9 will bring together the aerospace, space, defence, and internal security sectors on a single platform. Telangana is set to host Raksha Expo 2026—India’s first defence and aerospace expo organised by a state government—with the curtain-raiser scheduled to be held in Hyderabad on October 24. The main event, scheduled from December 7 to 9 at Bharat Future City, will bring together the aerospace, space, defence, and internal security sectors on a single platform to promote domestic manufacturing, innovation, and investment. “The nature of conflict is changing. Conventional methods of warfare and statecraft now operate alongside drones and new-age missiles. Telangana must be the centre of this revolution. We must be the largest contributors to India’s national and internal security,” Telangana chief minister A Revanth Reddy said. “Telangana must become the largest contributor to the mission of securing India’s national and internal security. I am confident Telangana will help make India a global defence superpower,” he said. The program The curtain-raiser is expected to bring together more than 80 leaders from over 70 organisations, including global original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and Indian defence and aerospace companies. Companies represented include Airbus, Boeing, Tata Lockheed Martin, Safran, Rolls-Royce and GE Aerospace, among others. Union defence minister Rajnath Singh has been invited to inaugurate the main expo. The state government has also planned a roadshow in New Delhi on October 29 to build participation ahead of the December summit. The expo will be held as a flagship event alongside the Invest Telangana Global Summit 2026. Its programme will include exhibitions, live technology demonstrations, drone shows and a planned air show on December 9. Business-to-business and business-to-government meetings are expected to connect manufacturers, startups, and micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) with government representatives, security agencies, and international investors. The aim is to enable supplier partnerships, joint ventures, technology transfer, and indigenous co-development. Hyderabad’s existing aerospace and defence ecosystem will be central to the showcase. The city is home to more than 12 Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) laboratories and defence public sector enterprises, as well as private manufacturers such as Tata Advanced Systems, Adani Defence and Bharat Forge. The Telangana Rising 2047 link The state’s aerospace network has produced 400 Apache helicopter fuselages. It also serves as the global single source for C-130J Super Hercules empennages— the structure at the rear of an aircraft responsible for aerodynamic stability. The event is also linked to the state’s Telangana Rising 2047 vision, which seeks to position Telangana as a major economic and manufacturing hub and achieve the status of a $1 trillion economy by 2034. “Hyderabad has powered India’s strategic programmes for decades, from missiles and fighter aircraft to satellites and secure communications, and is home to nearly 30 per cent of the country’s defence and aerospace industry,” said chief secretary Sanjay Jaju. The event comes amid a push to strengthen domestic defence manufacturing and reduce vulnerabilities in global supply chains. India’s defence production reached a record ₹ 1.78 lakh crore in 2025-26, while defence exports touched ₹ 38,424 crore. Telangana’s aerospace exports also rose from ₹ 15,900 crore in 2023-24 to ₹ 30,742 crore in 2024-25.

news.exam_corner_topic: Surveillance and 'constant paranoia': Western diplomats tell BBC of life in war-time Moscow
news.headline: Surveillance and 'constant paranoia': Western diplomats tell BBC of life in war-time Moscow
news.story_lead: Ex-US and French ambassadors Lynne Tracy and Pierre LÃ©vy were among those to speak to the BBC of their time in Moscow - Published 5 hours ago "Being the ambassador to Russia was probably the hardest assignment of my career," Lynne Tracy, who represented the US in Moscow from 2023 and 2025, tells the BBC. US, UK and European diplomats once played a crucial role in Russia, defusing tensions even at the worst moments of the Cold War. But now, deemed "unfriendly" by President Vladimir Putin's government, Western ambassadors are under constant surveillance, isolated and increasingly cut off from the country they were sent to understand, as the war in Ukraine grinds on through its fifth year.
news.full_article_text: Ex-US and French ambassadors Lynne Tracy and Pierre LÃ©vy were among those to speak to the BBC of their time in Moscow - Published 5 hours ago "Being the ambassador to Russia was probably the hardest assignment of my career," Lynne Tracy, who represented the US in Moscow from 2023 and 2025, tells the BBC. US, UK and European diplomats once played a crucial role in Russia, defusing tensions even at the worst moments of the Cold War. But now, deemed "unfriendly" by President Vladimir Putin's government, Western ambassadors are under constant surveillance, isolated and increasingly cut off from the country they were sent to understand, as the war in Ukraine grinds on through its fifth year. The BBC has spoken to five diplomats who have served in Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion. They compare current pressure levels to the Cold War era - when Western embassies were monitored through physical surveillance, listening devices hidden inside gifts , and "spy dust" - a near invisible chemical agent used to track officials. Hundreds of Russian diplomats were expelled from countries in Europe and the US after the war began in 2022. Moscow responded in kind, declaring hundreds of Western diplomats persona non grata and leaving many embassies short-staffed. Tracy's 30-year career took her to countries like Pakistan, where she survived an armed attack in 2008. But she says that even under constant physical threat, her posting in Peshawar was, in a sense, easier than Russia. "There, I still felt that there were things within my control. What made Moscow more difficult were the high levels of uncertainty." The constant pressure from Russian counterintelligence was the primary source of such uncertainty, she recalls. Tracy pictured leaving Russia's Foreign Ministry after being summoned by Moscow in 2023 Russian diplomats in the West also complain of such unfair treatment. But according to the diplomats who spoke to the BBC, the scope and tactics of Moscow's intelligence services are far greater. "Expect listening devices, expect cameras in every single room of your house," a former European diplomat says of the warning he received before leaving for Moscow. Another ex-ambassador says they were forced to dismiss two Russian employees after Moscow's domestic security service, the FSB, tried to recruit them, demanding that they report on everything going on at the diplomatic mission. The pair told the embassy instead, who let them go - "otherwise, they could have faced some sort of criminal prosecution". Meanwhile, Russians who would ordinarily build relationships with diplomatic staff - such as those working in academia and culture - are also being intimidated into avoiding contact with Western officials. One former ambassador says his guests were once "tailed" by FSB agents right up to the doors of the embassy. - Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia Published 4 days ago - Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage - and Russia is the chief suspect Published 4 September - They fled Russia, but the West sent them back Published 7 days ago Just this June, guests invited to the British ambassador's residence in Moscow for the King's birthday celebrations said they had been harassed by pro-Kremlin activists and state-media journalists, and then questioned by the police. One of the guests says he has since declined several invitations to events at Western embassies out of fear. Not everyone can deal with the pressure. One former ambassador says "constant paranoia" has driven a number of officials to quit their jobs. Even after leaving Russia himself, he adds, he was looking over his shoulder for months. 'Generals prove what they can do in war. The same is true for diplomats' In the immediate aftermath of the invasion, there were discussions across Europe about whether to recall ambassadors or stop working in Russia altogether, says former French ambassador Pierre LÃ©vy. He remembers calling Paris immediately to say pulling their envoys would be a mistake, feeling that the worse relations became, the more important they would be. The invasion quickly transformed their work, says another ex-European ambassador; the co-operation required for their usual efforts on bilateral relations, trade and joint projects was now impossible. And for those who stayed in Russia, the war left them with a host of new priorities beyond supporting their own citizens and companies. Firstly, countries viewed as unfriendly by Moscow still wanted at least some channel of communication with Russian officials to get an accurate picture of what was happening inside the country. But they also had to protect their staff and keep their embassies functioning. Pierre LÃ©vy (second from the left) and Lynne Tracy (second from the right) pictured at the funeral service for opposition leader Alexei Navalny in March 2024 After Russia's ban on hiring foreign nationals in 2021, the US embassy's facilities team was left significantly understaffed. Ðven a minor plumbing issue like a leaking pipe could turn into a major problem, draining the time of diplomatic workers. One diplomat recalls discussing staffing shortages with a Russian official, who advised him not to get too upset. "He said, 'at least you still have the chef'." Financial sanctions imposed by Western governments to support Ukraine created different day-to-day difficulties. news.exam_corner_topic: In a first, UN's Loss and Damage Fund sets aside $21.6 million for Nepal for Bhote Koshi disaster
news.headline: In a first, UN's Loss and Damage Fund sets aside $21.6 million for Nepal for Bhote Koshi disaster
news.story_lead: In a first, UN's Loss and Damage Fund sets aside $21.6 million for Nepal for Bhote Koshi disaster It is the first time money has been allocated to or set aside for a country since the fund's creation and marks a pivotal point. For the first time since it was operationalised at COP 28, the United Nations’ (UN) Loss and Damage Fund has provisionally approved $20 million plus $1.6 million in oversight fees for Nepal on Thursday for the damage caused during August’s Bhote Koshi River floods, which killed at least 1,000 people and left over 5,000 missing. The Board for the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) met at an “extraordinary meeting” on Thursday to address a formal climate-emergency funding request from Nepal for $20 million over a four-year period.
news.full_article_text: In a first, UN's Loss and Damage Fund sets aside $21.6 million for Nepal for Bhote Koshi disaster It is the first time money has been allocated to or set aside for a country since the fund's creation and marks a pivotal point. For the first time since it was operationalised at COP 28, the United Nations’ (UN) Loss and Damage Fund has provisionally approved $20 million plus $1.6 million in oversight fees for Nepal on Thursday for the damage caused during August’s Bhote Koshi River floods, which killed at least 1,000 people and left over 5,000 missing. The Board for the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) met at an “extraordinary meeting” on Thursday to address a formal climate-emergency funding request from Nepal for $20 million over a four-year period. This accounts for only around 0.7% of the costs estimated to be incurred by Nepal during the disaster. However, it is the first time money has been allocated to or set aside for a country since the fund's creation and marks a pivotal point in developing countries' efforts to access climate finance for disasters. The Loss and Damage Fund was set up to provide financial assistance to developing countries that are especially vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change – helping them cope with unavoidable economic and non-economic losses Experts said Nepal will still have to formally apply for this funding, and the Board will consider the request at its next meeting in December. This is the maximum amount that can currently be requested for a single project. The funding is expected to cover about 0.7% of the costs of the August Nepal floods, which preliminary estimates suggest could be around US$2.56 billion. The co-chairs received a communication from the Government of Nepal via its senior signatory national focal point on August 31. Within the communication, Nepal requested that the Board “take a special decision to respond rapidly, directly and effectively in accordance with its Governing Instrument”. Applications and contributions So far, developing countries have submitted 176 applications to the fund, totalling $2.8 billion, a separate analysis by Carbon Brief shows. As of March 15 this year, the Loss and Damage Fund had received $822.06 million in pledges from 27 countries, with total grant contributions currently standing at $ 629.70 million. The largest contributors include the UAE ($100 million); Germany ($98.4 million); France ($ 53.07 million); the United Kingdom ($ 52.15 million); Spain ($ 44.01 million); and Australia ($ 34.11 million). Harjeet Singh, Global Convenor, Fill the Fund campaign and Founding Director, Satat Sampada Climate Foundation, said Thursday marked a historic day in responding to Nepal. “No country should have to endure a catastrophe and wait seven weeks, through historic letters and relentless pressure, just to unlock the Fund’s first-ever emergency meeting. We must set up a permanent rapid-response system that moves support in days, not months,” he said. Why it is a milestone For India and other developing countries facing similar climate-induced disasters, this remains an important milestone in accessing disaster finance, experts said. Anjal Prakash, Professor of Public Policy at FLAME University and an IPCC author, said Nepal’s allocation was an important recognition of the need to pay for climate justice. “However, setting money aside is not the same as delivering it. At just 0.7% of estimated losses, this support exposes the enormous gap between climate impacts and available finance. The priority must now be rapid disbursement, with transparent safeguards that enable rather than delay assistance. We need a permanent emergency window, simpler access procedures and predictable contributions from wealthy countries,” he said, stating recovery support should reach affected families, restore essential services and protect livelihoods without adding to national debt. “Ahead of COP31, the test is delivery- whether this decision becomes a reliable system that responds to vulnerable communities at the speed and scale their losses demand, rather than another symbolic financial commitment,” he added. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Jasjeev Gandhiok Jasjeev Gandhiok is an Assistant Editor with Hindustan Times, where he covers environment, climate change, the clean energy transition and wildlife at the National Bureau. Gandhiok has over a decade of experience in journalism and is based in Delhi. He has reported extensively on Delhi and the National Capital Region (NCR). This includes the region's air pollution woes, a polluted Yamuna and on urban wildlife still thriving in the region. He joined HT in October 2021. Prior to that, he had five-year stint at The Times of India in Delhi, where he also covered Delhi, with a focus on environment and wildlife. Gandhiok has covered some recent events around the Capital too, ranging from the farmers' protests, the northeast Delhi riots and the CAA-NRC protests, reporting from the ground on all of these. He also travels across the country to report on how environment and climate change impact everyday life, while also writing on endangered species. His reports in 2019 on toxic leachate from Delhi's landfills led to the National Green Tribunal (NGT) taking suo motu cognisance and ultimately asking the state government to start bio-mining to flatten and remove all three landfills in the capital. He also closely tracks the implementation of government policies on climate, renewable energy and environmental protection. His focus remains on impactful, public-interest journalism which explains how environmental decisions affect people's everyday lives. Read More

For the first time since it was operationalised at COP 28, the United Nations’ (UN) Loss and Damage Fund has provisionally approved $20 million plus $1.6 million in oversight fees for Nepal on Thursday for the damage caused during August’s Bhote Koshi River floods, which killed at least 1,000 people and left over 5,000 missing.

The Board for the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) met at an “extraordinary meeting” on Thursday to address a formal climate-emergency funding request from Nepal for $20 million over a four-year period.

This accounts for only around 0.7% of the costs estimated to be incurred by Nepal during the disaster. However, it is the first time money has been allocated to or set aside for a country since the fund's creation and marks a pivotal point in developing countries' efforts to access climate finance for disasters.

The Loss and Damage Fund was set up to provide financial assistance to developing countries that are especially vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change – helping them cope with unavoidable economic and non-economic losses

hindi_translation.headline: In a first, UN's Loss and Damage Fund sets aside $21.6 million for Nepal for Bhote Koshi disaster
hindi_translation.story_lead: In a first, UN's Loss and Damage Fund sets aside $21.6 million for Nepal for Bhote Koshi disaster It is the first time money has been allocated to or set aside for a country since the fund's creation and marks a pivotal point. For the first time since it was operationalised at COP 28, the United Nations’ (UN) Loss and Damage Fund has provisionally approved $20 million plus $1.6 million in oversight fees for Nepal on Thursday for the damage caused during August’s Bhote Koshi River floods, which killed at least 1,000 people and left over 5,000 missing. The Board for the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) met at an “extraordinary meeting” on Thursday to address a formal climate-emergency funding request from Nepal for $20 million over a four-year period.
hindi_translation.full_article_text: In a first, UN's Loss and Damage Fund sets aside $21.6 million for Nepal for Bhote Koshi disaster It is the first time money has been allocated to or set aside for a country since the fund's creation and marks a pivotal point. For the first time since it was operationalised at COP 28, the United Nations’ (UN) Loss and Damage Fund has provisionally approved $20 million plus $1.6 million in oversight fees for Nepal on Thursday for the damage caused during August’s Bhote Koshi River floods, which killed at least 1,000 people and left over 5,000 missing. The Board for the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) met at an “extraordinary meeting” on Thursday to address a formal climate-emergency funding request from Nepal for $20 million over a four-year period. This accounts for only around 0.7% of the costs estimated to be incurred by Nepal during the disaster. However, it is the first time money has been allocated to or set aside for a country since the fund's creation and marks a pivotal point in developing countries' efforts to access climate finance for disasters. The Loss and Damage Fund was set up to provide financial assistance to developing countries that are especially vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change – helping them cope with unavoidable economic and non-economic losses Experts said Nepal will still have to formally apply for this funding, and the Board will consider the request at its next meeting in December. This is the maximum amount that can currently be requested for a single project. The funding is expected to cover about 0.7% of the costs of the August Nepal floods, which preliminary estimates suggest could be around US$2.56 billion. The co-chairs received a communication from the Government of Nepal via its senior signatory national focal point on August 31. Within the communication, Nepal requested that the Board “take a special decision to respond rapidly, directly and effectively in accordance with its Governing Instrument”. Applications and contributions So far, developing countries have submitted 176 applications to the fund, totalling $2.8 billion, a separate analysis by Carbon Brief shows. As of March 15 this year, the Loss and Damage Fund had received $822.06 million in pledges from 27 countries, with total grant contributions currently standing at $ 629.70 million. The largest contributors include the UAE ($100 million); Germany ($98.4 million); France ($ 53.07 million); the United Kingdom ($ 52.15 million); Spain ($ 44.01 million); and Australia ($ 34.11 million). Harjeet Singh, Global Convenor, Fill the Fund campaign and Founding Director, Satat Sampada Climate Foundation, said Thursday marked a historic day in responding to Nepal. “No country should have to endure a catastrophe and wait seven weeks, through historic letters and relentless pressure, just to unlock the Fund’s first-ever emergency meeting. We must set up a permanent rapid-response system that moves support in days, not months,” he said. Why it is a milestone For India and other developing countries facing similar climate-induced disasters, this remains an important milestone in accessing disaster finance, experts said. Anjal Prakash, Professor of Public Policy at FLAME University and an IPCC author, said Nepal’s allocation was an important recognition of the need to pay for climate justice. “However, setting money aside is not the same as delivering it. At just 0.7% of estimated losses, this support exposes the enormous gap between climate impacts and available finance. The priority must now be rapid disbursement, with transparent safeguards that enable rather than delay assistance. We need a permanent emergency window, simpler access procedures and predictable contributions from wealthy countries,” he said, stating recovery support should reach affected families, restore essential services and protect livelihoods without adding to national debt. “Ahead of COP31, the test is delivery- whether this decision becomes a reliable system that responds to vulnerable communities at the speed and scale their losses demand, rather than another symbolic financial commitment,” he added. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Jasjeev Gandhiok Jasjeev Gandhiok is an Assistant Editor with Hindustan Times, where he covers environment, climate change, the clean energy transition and wildlife at the National Bureau. Gandhiok has over a decade of experience in journalism and is based in Delhi. He has reported extensively on Delhi and the National Capital Region (NCR). This includes the region's air pollution woes, a polluted Yamuna and on urban wildlife still thriving in the region. He joined HT in October 2021. Prior to that, he had five-year stint at The Times of India in Delhi, where he also covered Delhi, with a focus on environment and wildlife. Gandhiok has covered some recent events around the Capital too, ranging from the farmers' protests, the northeast Delhi riots and the CAA-NRC protests, reporting from the ground on all of these. He also travels across the country to report on how environment and climate change impact everyday life, while also writing on endangered species. His reports in 2019 on toxic leachate from Delhi's landfills led to the National Green Tribunal (NGT) taking suo motu cognisance and ultimately asking the state government to start bio-mining to flatten and remove all three landfills in the capital. He also closely tracks the implementation of government policies on climate, renewable energy and environmental protection. His focus remains on impactful, public-interest journalism which explains how environmental decisions affect people's everyday lives. Read More

news.headline: CPI(M) MP Demands Independent Probe into Exposure of SBI Customer Data on Dark Web
news.story_lead: CPI(M) Member of Parliament A A Rahim has written to Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman requesting an independent investigation into the exposure of 3,897 State Bank of India customer records on the dark web. The lawmaker emphasized that even though primary banking operations remain unaffected, compromised personal financial information poses severe risks to account holders and warrants urgent institutional intervention.
news.full_article_text:
State Bank of India (SBI) formally notified the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) and the National Stock Exchange (NSE) on October 21 regarding a data security incident involving customer information. The bank disclosed that 3,897 customer records containing sensitive personal information were identified within a larger dataset of approximately 3.75 lakh records circulating on the dark web. The exposed information reportedly includes registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, names, gender, email addresses, residential addresses, branch details, Customer Information File (CIF) identifiers, lead IDs, and metadata associated with loan files and related records.

SBI became aware of the data breach on October 16 after receiving alerts from its threat intelligence provider, the Defence Cyber Agency, and the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In). Although the state-run lender stated that its core operational systems remain completely functional and uncompromised, CPI(M) MP A A Rahim addressed a formal letter to Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman on October 21 demanding urgent government action.

In his representation, MP Rahim highlighted concerns regarding cybersecurity readiness and data protection protocols across public sector banks. He asserted that the uninterrupted functioning of banking operations does not reduce the seriousness of customer privacy leaks. The MP urged the Union Finance Ministry to launch a time-bound independent investigation to identify the origin and extent of the leak, direct SBI to directly inform affected customers, establish accessible reporting channels for suspected fraud, and fix strict accountability for security lapses. He warned that affected customers could become targets for identity theft, phishing schemes, financial impersonation, and fraudulent exploitation.

While operational continuity was maintained, the leak of granular personal data poses severe cybersecurity and fraud risks for individual account holders. It underlines the necessity for mandatory breach notification rules, robust data protection mechanisms, and comprehensive security audits across India's financial sector.

hindi_translation.headline: एसबीआई ग्राहक डेटा लीक मामले में सीपीआई(एम) सांसद ने वित्त मंत्री से स्वतंत्र जांच की मांग की
hindi_translation.story_lead: सीपीआई(एम) सांसद ए ए रहीम ने केंद्रीय वित्त मंत्री निर्मला सीतारमण को पत्र लिखकर डार्क वेब पर भारतीय स्टेट बैंक के 3,897 ग्राहकों के रिकॉर्ड उजागर होने की स्वतंत्र जांच की मांग की है। सांसद ने जोर दिया कि भले ही मुख्य बैंकिंग परिचालन अप्रभावित रहे हों, लेकिन व्यक्तिगत वित्तीय जानकारी के लीक होने से ग्राहकों के लिए गंभीर जोखिम पैदा होता है और इसके लिए तत्काल संस्थागत कदम उठाने की आवश्यकता है।
hindi_translation.full_article_text:
भारतीय स्टेट बैंक (एसबीआई) ने 21 अक्टूबर को बॉम्बे स्टॉक एक्सचेंज (बीएसई) और नेशनल स्टॉक एक्सचेंज (एनएसई) को ग्राहक डेटा से जुड़ी एक सुरक्षा घटना की औपचारिक जानकारी दी। बैंक ने खुलासा किया कि डार्क वेब पर घूम रहे लगभग 3.75 लाख रिकॉर्ड्स के एक बड़े सेट में 3,897 एसबीआई ग्राहक रिकॉर्ड पाए गए जिनमें संवेदनशील व्यक्तिगत जानकारी शामिल थी। उजागर हुई जानकारी में पंजीकृत मोबाइल नंबर, जन्म तिथि, नाम, लिंग, ईमेल पते, आवासीय पते, शाखा विवरण, ग्राहक सूचना फाइल (सीआईएफ) पहचानकर्ता, लीड आईडी और ऋण रिकॉर्ड से जुड़े मेटाडेटा शामिल बताए गए हैं।

एसबीआई को 16 अक्टूबर को प्रदाता थ्रेट इंटेलिजेंस, डिफेंस साइबर एजेंसी और इंडियन कंप्यूटर इमरजेंसी रिस्पॉन्स टीम (सीईआरटी-इन) से अलर्ट मिलने के बाद इस डेटा लीक का पता चला। यद्यपि सार्वजनिक क्षेत्र के इस बैंक ने कहा कि उसका मुख्य बैंकिंग परिचालन पूरी तरह से सुरक्षित और अप्रभावित रहा, सीपीआई(एम) सांसद ए ए रहीम ने 21 अक्टूबर को वित्त मंत्री निर्मला सीतारमण को पत्र भेजकर तत्काल सरकारी हस्तक्षेप की मांग की।

अपने पत्र में सांसद रहीम ने सार्वजनिक क्षेत्र के बैंकों में साइबर सुरक्षा तैयारियों और डेटा सुरक्षा प्रोटोकॉल को लेकर चिंता व्यक्त की। उन्होंने तर्क दिया कि बैंकिंग सेवाओं में व्यवधान न आने से ग्राहकों की व्यक्तिगत जानकारी के उजागर होने की गंभीरता कम नहीं हो जाती। सांसद ने वित्त मंत्रालय से मांग की कि वह इस लीक के स्रोत और सीमा की पहचान के लिए समयबद्ध स्वतंत्र जांच कराए, एसबीआई को सीधे प्रभावित ग्राहकों को सूचित करने का निर्देश दे, संदिग्ध धोखाधड़ी की रिपोर्टिंग के लिए सुलभ चैनल स्थापित करे और सुरक्षा चूक के लिए कड़ी जवाबदेही तय करे। उन्होंने चेतावनी दी कि प्रभावित ग्राहक पहचान की चोरी, लक्षित फ़िशिंग, वित्तीय धोखाधड़ी और शोषण का शिकार हो सकते हैं।
bullet_points: एसबीआई ने 21 अक्टूबर को बीएसई और एनएसई को ग्राहक डेटा सुरक्षा घटना के बारे में सूचित किया।
डार्क वेब पर 3.75 लाख रिकॉर्ड के बड़े सेट में एसबीआई के 3,897 ग्राहक रिकॉर्ड की पहचान की गई।
लीक हुए डेटा में नाम, मोबाइल नंबर, जन्म तिथि, लिंग, ईमेल, आवासीय पता, सीआईएफ आईडी और लोन मेटाडेटा शामिल हैं।
एसबीआई को 16 अक्टूबर को सीईआरटी-इन, डिफेंस साइबर एजेंसी और थ्रेट इंटेलिजेंस प्रदाता से घटना की जानकारी मिली।
बैंक ने स्पष्ट किया कि उसके मुख्य बैंकिंग परिचालन पर कोई प्रभाव नहीं पड़ा है।
सीपीआई(एम) सांसद ए ए रहीम ने 21 अक्टूबर को वित्त मंत्री निर्मला सीतारमण को स्वतंत्र जांच के लिए पत्र लिखा।
रहीम ने प्रभावित ग्राहकों को सीधी सूचना देने, धोखाधड़ी रिपोर्टिंग चैनल स्थापित करने और सख्त जवाबदेही तय करने की मांग की।
सांसद ने चेतावनी दी कि प्रभावित नागरिक पहचान की चोरी, फ़िशिंग और वित्तीय धोखाधड़ी के खतरे में हैं।

डार्क वेब डेटासेट का कुल आकार: लगभग 3.75 लाख रिकॉर्ड।
अधिसूचित स्टॉक एक्सचेंज: बीएसई और एनएसई।

news.headline: Kolkata Durga Puja Stampede: SIT Identifies Narrow Exits and Dim Lighting as Primary Triggers
news.story_lead: A six-member Special Investigation Team (SIT) investigating the fatal October 17 Durga Puja stampede in Kolkata has identified severe crowd-flow bottlenecks, inadequate lighting, and false loudspeaker announcements as core factors behind the tragedy. The incident at the Chor Bagan pandal resulted in 19 deaths and left 25 individuals injured on the Saptami day of the festival. Police have detained eight individuals under key provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).
news.full_article_text:
A six-member Special Investigation Team (SIT), headed by retired Calcutta High Court judge Anindita Roy Saraswati, has identified structural bottlenecks and operational lapses as key factors behind the October 17 stampede at the Chor Bagan Durga Puja pandal in north Kolkata. The tragedy took place on Saptami, the seventh day of the festival, claiming 19 lives and injuring 25 people during heavy rainfall and intense crowd surging.

Preliminary findings by the SIT confirm that the stampede occurred at the exit point rather than inside the pandal itself. Investigators highlighted that common visitors were funneled into a single, dimly lit exit pathway measuring approximately seven feet in width. This egress route was further constricted by installed outdoor air conditioning compressor units and temporary food stalls along the lane. Furthermore, access to the primary view of the idol required visitors to navigate a five-foot-wide circular ramp, which lacked alternative evacuation routes.

Witness reports and police findings indicate that the emergency gate, typically designated for VIP movement, remained locked during the surge. The immediate trigger for the stampede appears to have been an unverified announcement over the public address system claiming that the pandal structure was collapsing, prompting widespread panic among the crowd trying to descend from the ramp.

Law enforcement officials have taken eight individuals into custody in connection with the incident, including puja committee secretary Raj Kumar Sewda, vice-president Santanu Dubey, and committee member Sanjib Raha, who was identified as one of the individuals who made the panicky announcement over the loudspeaker. All accused have been charged under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) Sections 105 (culpable homicide not amounting to murder), 110 (attempt to commit culpable homicide), and 3(5) (acts done by several persons in furtherance of common intention). Seven of the accused were remanded to 10-day police custody.

To recreate the scene and establish accountability, police forensic teams conducted 3D spatial mapping and deployed drone aerial surveillance around the pandal and adjacent narrow lanes. The incident has also sparked a political controversy in West Bengal, with opposition parties criticizing the administration and pointing to political figures associated as patrons with the event management committee. West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari visited the affected families, announcing financial compensation and a state government employment pledge for one family member of each deceased victim.
news.background_context: West Bengal has no recent history of fatal stampedes occurring at Durga Puja pandals, making the October 17 tragedy at Chor Bagan an unprecedented crowd management crisis during the state's largest cultural festival.

hindi_translation.headline: कोलकाता दुर्गा पूजा भगदड़: एसआईटी ने संकीर्ण निकास और कम रोशनी को मुख्य कारण बताया
hindi_translation.story_lead: कोलकाता के चोर बगान पंडाल में 17 अक्टूबर को हुई घातक दुर्गा पूजा भगदड़ की जांच कर रही छह सदस्यीय विशेष जांच टीम (SIT) ने भीड़ नियंत्रण की कमियों, अपर्याप्त रोशनी और लाउडस्पीकर से की गई झूठी घोषणाओं को इस त्रासदी का मुख्य कारण माना है। सप्तमी के दिन हुई इस घटना में 19 लोगों की मौत हो गई थी और 25 लोग घायल हुए थे। पुलिस ने भारतीय न्याय संहिता (BNS) की धाराओं के तहत आठ लोगों को हिरासत में लिया है।
hindi_translation.full_article_text:
कलकत्ता उच्च न्यायालय की सेवानिवृत्त न्यायाधीश अनिंदिता रॉय सरस्वती के नेतृत्व में छह सदस्यीय विशेष जांच टीम (SIT) ने उत्तर कोलकाता के चोर बगान दुर्गा पूजा पंडाल में 17 अक्टूबर को हुई भगदड़ के पीछे ढांचागत कमियों और परिचालनगत चूक की पहचान की है। यह हादसा त्यौहार के सातवें दिन (सप्तमी) को भारी बारिश और भीड़ के दबाव के दौरान हुआ, जिसमें 19 लोगों की जान चली गई और 25 अन्य घायल हो गए।

एसआईटी के शुरुआती निष्कर्षों से पुष्टि होती है कि भगदड़ पंडाल के अंदर नहीं बल्कि निकास बिंदु पर हुई थी। जांचकर्ताओं ने पाया कि आम आगंतुकों को लगभग सात फीट चौड़े और कम रोशनी वाले एक ही निकास मार्ग से निकाला जा रहा था। पंडाल के भीतर लगी एयर कंडीशनर मशीनों की बाहरी इकाइयों और सड़क पर लगी खाद्य दुकानों के कारण यह निकास मार्ग और अधिक संकरा हो गया था। इसके अलावा, मूर्ति के 360-डिग्री दर्शन के लिए पांच फीट चौड़े और सात फीट ऊंचे गोलाकार रैंप से गुजरना पड़ता था, जहां से बाहर निकलने का कोई वैकल्पिक रास्ता नहीं था।

प्रत्यक्षदर्शियों और पुलिस जांच के अनुसार, वीआईपी आवाजाही के लिए इस्तेमाल होने वाला आपातकालीन गेट घटना के दौरान बंद था। भगदड़ की तात्कालिक वजह लाउडस्पीकर के माध्यम से की गई एक अप्रमाणित घोषणा बनी, जिसमें दावा किया गया था कि पंडाल का ढांचा ढहने वाला है। इस घोषणा से रैंप पर मौजूद लोगों में दहशत फैल गई और वे जान बचाने के लिए भागने लगे।

पुलिस ने इस मामले में आठ लोगों को गिरफ्तार या हिरासत में लिया है, जिनमें पूजा समिति के सचिव राज कुमार सेवड़ा, उपाध्यक्ष शांतनु दुबे और समिति सदस्य संजीब राहा शामिल हैं। संजीब राहा पर लाउडस्पीकर से घबराहट फैलाने वाली घोषणा करने का आरोप है। सभी आरोपियों पर भारतीय न्याय संहिता (BNS) की धारा 105 (गैर-इरादतन हत्या), 110 (गैर-इरादतन हत्या का प्रयास) और 3(5) (समान मंशा से किया गया अपराध) के तहत मामला दर्ज किया गया है। सात आरोपियों को 10 दिनों की पुलिस हिरासत में भेज दिया गया है।

घटनास्थल के पुनर्निर्माण और जिम्मेदारी तय करने के लिए, पुलिस फोरेंसिक टीमों ने 3D मैपिंग की और ड्रोन कैमरों से पंडाल और आसपास की संकरी गलियों का हवाई सर्वेक्षण किया। इस घटना ने पश्चिम बंगाल में राजनीतिक विवाद भी खड़ा कर दिया है। राज्य के मुख्यमंत्री शुभेंदु अधिकारी ने पीड़ित परिवारों से मुलाकात की और प्रत्येक मृतक के परिवार के एक सदस्य को राज्य सरकार में नौकरी और वित्तीय मुआवजे का वादा किया है।
hindi_translation.background_context: पश्चिम बंगाल में दुर्गा पूजा पंडालों में भगदड़ से मौत की कोई हालिया इतिहास नहीं रही है, जिसके कारण चोर बगान की यह घटना राज्य के सबसे बड़े सांस्कृतिक उत्सव के दौरान एक अभूतपूर्व भीड़ प्रबंधन संकट बन गई है।
bullet_points: सेवानिवृत्त न्यायाधीश अनिंदिता रॉय सरस्वती के नेतृत्व में 6 सदस्यीय एसआईटी चोर बगान पंडाल भगदड़ की जांच कर रही है।
17 अक्टूबर (सप्तमी) को हुई इस त्रासदी में 19 लोगों की मौत हुई और 25 घायल हुए।
जांच से पता चला है कि भगदड़ संकीर्ण 7-फीट निकास मार्ग पर हुई, जो दुकानों और एसी इकाइयों से घिरा था।
वीआईपी आपातकालीन गेट बंद रखा गया था, जिससे आगंतुकों के पास बाहर निकलने का कोई दूसरा रास्ता नहीं था।
लाउडस्पीकर पर ढांचा ढहने की झूठी अफवाह के बाद भीड़ में भगदड़ मच गई।
पूजा आयोजक समिति के प्रमुख सदस्यों सहित आठ लोगों को गिरफ्तार/हिरासत में लिया गया है।
आरोपियों पर बीएनएस की धारा 105, 110 और 3(5) के तहत मामले दर्ज किए गए हैं।
फोरेंसिक टीम ने 3D मैपिंग और ड्रोन कैमरों से स्थल का विश्लेषण किया।
राज्य सरकार ने पीड़ितों के परिवारों को वित्तीय सहायता और नौकरी देने की घोषणा की है।

news.headline: Civic Movement Led by 'Student List' Challenges 12-Year Rule of Aleksandar Vučić in Serbia
news.story_lead: Serbia is conducting snap parliamentary elections following two years of widespread anti-government protests triggered by a fatal infrastructure collapse in Novi Sad. Long-serving leader Aleksandar Vučić faces a significant political challenge from the 'Student List-Students Win' civic movement, which unites diverse socio-professional groups despite concerns over electoral fairness and state media bias.
news.full_article_text:
### Electoral Context and Political Landscape
Serbia's political landscape faces a critical turning point as citizens prepare for snap parliamentary elections. The election serves as a pivotal juncture for President Aleksandar Vučić, who has dominated Serbian politics for 12 years as Prime Minister, President, or Deputy Prime Minister since 2012. Having completed two terms as president, Vučić is leading his ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) with the goal of regaining the Prime Minister's office.

### Genesis of the Protests: The Novi Sad Tragedy
The political momentum shifted on 1 November 2024 when a concrete canopy collapsed at the railway station in Novi Sad, Serbia's second-largest city, resulting in 16 deaths. Public outrage focused on allegations of systemic corruption, official negligence, and poor oversight linked to the station's renovation project. The incident sparked student-led campus and street demonstrations, which subsequently expanded into a national civic movement involving farmers, actors, judges, and academics, organized via decentralized student plenums.

### Electoral System and Key Candidates
Serbia's legislative framework operates as a single national constituency with 250 parliamentary seats chosen under proportional representation with a 3% threshold. Out of 18 contesting lists, 7 are running a complete candidate slate for the 6.45 million registered voters.

The prominent opposition force, 'Student List-Students Win', features a non-partisan roster of professionals rather than active students. Key candidates include lead candidate Dr. Ilija Srdanović (a cardiology professor from Novi Sad), Dejan Bodiroga (former basketball player), Tihomir Stanić (actor), and Dejan Šoškić (former Governor of the National Bank of Serbia).

### Platform and Integrity Issues
The Student List's 11-point platform focuses on creating a specialized anti-corruption police unit, purging ministry officials linked to abuses or organized crime, ensuring public broadcast neutrality, and stopping political appointments in state enterprises. Independent observers, including CRTA and the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), have cited media imbalances, electoral engineering, and over 160 reported attacks on media workers during the year.
news.background_context: On 1 November 2024, a concrete canopy collapsed at the Novi Sad train station in Serbia, causing 16 deaths. The tragedy catalyzed anti-government protests against state corruption and administrative negligence, eventually causing the prime minister's resignation and large-scale demonstrations in Belgrade in March 2025.
